Inflation remains elevated, reflecting pandemic-era supply/demand imbalances, higher food and energy prices, and broader price pressures; in response, the FOMC raised the federal funds rate to 4.25–4.50% and signaled “ongoing increases,” while continuing balance‑sheet runoff. This stance is consistent with Taylor‑rule style prescriptions when inflation runs well above the 2% objective (Fed “implements Taylor Rule”) and with evidence from Romer and Romer that credible tightening curbs inflation but transmits to real activity with lags—explicitly acknowledged in the statement. The operational details—raising interest on reserves to 4.4% and setting ON RRP at 4.3%—reflect the post‑2008 floor‑system toolkit (interest on reserves) used to steer short rates. Forward guidance (“ongoing increases” alongside data‑dependence) works through expectations and the term structure, in line with term‑premium/expectations channels highlighted in the literature (e.g., Cochrane–Piazzesi), amplifying tightening beyond the front end. Continuing QT is the mirror of QE’s duration/term‑premium effects and reinforces restrictive financial conditions. While war- and pandemic‑related supply shocks are less directly addressable by monetary policy, the emphasis on returning inflation to target aligns with inflation‑targeting/credibility research and the Fed’s 2020 average‑inflation framework pivot.

Overall tone: hawkish due to elevated inflation and a tightening bias, modestly tempered by recognition of cumulative tightening and policy lags. sentiment score = -0.15
